So what: The BOT structure means plant economics resemble infrastructure/utility financing (bond-funded, long-duration, government-counterparty risk) rather than industrial manufacturing, which shapes how to value the listed operators.
The major publicly listed operators building and running China's waste-to-energy plants under the BOT model include China Everbright, Chongqing Sanfeng, Shanghai Environment Protection Group, and Zheneng Jinjiang Environment, with over 20 publicly listed companies total in the space.

The central government's December 2017 order for provincial governments to finish site selection by 2018 - timed against a national target of 591,000 tons/day capacity by 2020 and the fact that a plant takes 15-24 months to build - created a hard construction deadline that turned a steady pipeline (41 new plants/year from 2013-2017) into a rush of over 400 projects in progress by mid-2019.

Incinerators are most notorious for emitting dioxins and furans - a family of roughly 75 dioxins and 135 furans, chlorinated hydrocarbons formed by burning chlorinated plastics, that resist environmental breakdown and bioaccumulate in livestock and food, causing reproductive problems, weakened immune systems, and potential cancers in people.

NIMBY politics and the Hangzhou playbook 4
In May 2014, a planned 3,000-ton/day incinerator in Hangzhou's Yuhang district - announced without prior public consultation after a 20,000-signature protest petition was ignored - triggered a mass clash between tens of thousands of protesters and police, including a blocked highway and hand-to-hand combat, forcing the government to suspend the project.

Academics describe the Hangzhou failure pattern as 'Decide-Announce-Defend' - technocratic site selection made without transparency, followed by a public announcement, followed by the government being forced to defend the decision against backlash - jokingly extended to 'Decide-Announce-Defend-Abandon' given how often it fails.

After the 2014 backlash, Hangzhou rebooted the project by replacing the inexperienced original state-owned operator with China Everbright, running a full participatory Environmental Impact Analysis that interviewed over 25,000 residents and collected 500 suggestions, hiring local residents as plant supervisors, and bussing 5,000 residents to tour existing Everbright facilities - construction restarted in April 2015 and the plant opened in November 2017, establishing the standard playbook for handling incinerator NIMBYism in China.
framework🗣 narratorconviction: highHangzhouChina Everbright

China's most infamous solid-waste disaster was not an incinerator but a landfill: in December 2015, landfilled construction waste in Shenzhen slid down as an avalanche, killing at least 73 people - an event frequently cited as justification for shifting from open landfilling toward incineration.

Origins of Indexing at Wells Fargo & the Birth of Dimensional 3
David Booth started at Wells Fargo's trust department in September 1971, the same month the firm launched its first indexed portfolio (the Samsonite account), working alongside outside consultants Fisher Black and Myron Scholes while they simultaneously developed the Black-Scholes option pricing model.

The S&P 500 index fund built inside Wells Fargo's trust department by the same group Booth worked in was later sold off multiple times and eventually became the cornerstone of what is now BlackRock's indexing business.

So what: Traces a direct lineage from a single early-1970s Wells Fargo project to the largest asset manager in the world today, useful context for understanding index-fund industry history and consolidation.

Dimensional Fund Advisors was founded in 1981 after Booth's original Wells Fargo group was shut down, reuniting Booth with Myron Scholes, Merton Miller, Gene Fama, and his old boss Mac McQuown to build a new firm.

Dimensional launched in 1981 with only a small-cap fund and immediately entered the worst 9-year stretch of relative small-cap performance on record, with small stocks underperforming large stocks by the widest margin ever measured over a 9-year period.

The Fama-French Three-Factor Model & Value Investing 2
The Fama-French three-factor model — adding size (large vs. small) and value (value vs. growth) factors to the market factor — replaced the single-factor CAPM/beta framework around 1991-92 and is, three decades later, still regarded as the last major theoretical breakthrough in investing.
framework🗣 David Boothconviction: highFama-French three-factor modelGene FamaKen FrenchCAPM
So what: A reminder that the multi-factor framework underlying most modern factor investing (size, value) has gone essentially unchallenged as the dominant academic model for over 30 years.
“There's more than just the market. There's a size factor large versus small and then value versus growth.” ▶ 16:39
Dimensional began seeding its value strategies based on a September 1991 pre-publication draft of the Fama-French paper that Booth personally carried to a client and to Fama's office, launching the funds before the research was formally published.
data_point🗣 David Boothconviction: highDimensional Fund AdvisorsFama-French three-factor modelGene FamaKen French
So what: Illustrates a genuine information edge from proximity to primary academic research — DFA moved on the factor before the wider market had access to the published paper.
“the value strategy started uh before the uh paper was published by Fama and French” ▶ 17:17

Booth's rule of thumb for investor patience is that any sound strategy takes at least one year longer to pay off than an investor is willing to give it, meaning investors should mentally pre-commit to a longer holding period than feels comfortable.
framework🗣 David Boothconviction: highDavid Booth

Dimensional tells clients that the danger in fund selection is not the buy decision but the absence of a defined sell rule, since the natural temptation is to sell precisely when a fund underperforms — which could be this year, six years from now, or twenty years from now.
framework🗣 David Boothconviction: highDimensional Fund Advisors

Special Grand Jury Mechanics 2
Special federal grand juries, created by the 1970 Organized Crime Control Act, can serve up to 36 months versus roughly 18-24 months for an ordinary grand jury, making them the preferred vehicle for long-running, complex investigations.
data_point🗣 Anna Bowerconviction: highOrganized Crime Control ActDOJ
So what: A 3-year tenure signals prosecutors are set up for a multi-year investigative process, useful for gauging how long a politically charged legal overhang could persist rather than resolve quickly.
“a special grand jury, again, usually impanled for 18 months, but that can be extended up to 36 months” ▶ 3:31
Unlike ordinary grand juries, a federal special grand jury can issue a public report at the end of its term -- a rare statutory exception to normal grand jury secrecy -- giving prosecutors a way to publicize findings even without an indictment.
framework🗣 Anna Bowerconviction: highDOJ18 U.S.C. 3331-3333
So what: Analysts tracking politically charged investigations should watch for a report (not just an indictment) as a potential narrative-moving output tied to named individuals or institutions.
“special grand juries under the statute have the ability to submit a report at the end of their service” ▶ 4:22

Report-Writing Statute's Narrow Legal Limits 2
The federal special grand jury report statute is legally narrow: a 'general criminal conditions' report cannot name individuals, and a report naming a specific person for noncriminal misconduct must tie to organized criminal activity and can only target current (not former) appointed federal officials or employees as grounds for removal or discipline.
framework🗣 Anna Bowerconviction: highDOJ18 U.S.C. 3331-3333
So what: These statutory limits make it legally difficult to use a DC special grand jury report to publicly implicate former officials like James Comey, John Brennan or Jack Smith, tempering near-term reputational risk to those individuals from a report specifically (as opposed to a criminal indictment).
“the noncriminal misconduct that's alleged in the report about a named person has to be about someone who is an appointed public officer or employee” ▶ 27:08
Because the report provision can only name current appointed federal officials as grounds for removal or discipline, Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell is effectively the only prominent perceived Trump adversary who is legally eligible to be named in such a report.

So what: Powell, and by extension the Fed, remains a uniquely exposed legal target relative to other perceived adversaries -- directly relevant to monitoring political risk around Fed leadership and independence.

Grand Jury as a Standalone Pressure Tool 2
Even without an indictment or a published report, a three-year special grand jury can function as a standalone pressure mechanism -- issuing subpoenas, compelling repeated testimony, and creating perjury exposure from inconsistent answers -- so its mere existence carries legal and political risk for targets regardless of the ultimate outcome.

Historical Precedent: Rocky Flats 1
The only modern precedent for a federal special grand jury report -- the Rocky Flats nuclear-plant environmental case in Colorado -- ended with the judge rejecting the grand jury's report for failing statutory requirements, years of follow-on litigation, and grand jurors publicly accusing the Justice Department of a cover-up.
